title: 5 Skyscrapers That Cheat Physics (And How They Get Away With It)
short_cta: Want four more buildings that cheat physics? Watch the full video on Simply Weird, and follow for more weird stuff!

intro.say: Skyscrapers are not supposed to stand still. Wind shoves them, earthquakes shake them, and the taller they get, the more they want to wobble.
So engineers got sneaky. Giant swinging balls. Secret repairs at midnight. Buildings shaped to confuse the wind.
Here are five skyscrapers that cheat physics, and exactly how they get away with it.

chapters.title: Taipei 101 hides a giant steel ball
chapters.short_title: Why Taipei 101 Hides a 660-Ton Steel Ball

beats.say: There is a giant golden ball hanging inside this skyscraper, and nobody lost it there by accident.
Taipei 101 stands in a city that gets typhoons and earthquakes, so the tower is always being pushed around.
Tall buildings sway a little in strong wind. That is normal, but too much swaying makes people inside feel seasick.
So engineers hung a steel ball weighing about six hundred sixty metric tons between the eighty seventh and ninety second floors.
It is about eighteen feet wide, built from forty one thick steel plates stacked together like a giant hamburger.
When the wind pushes the tower one way, the ball swings the other way and pulls the building back toward the middle.
Engineers call this a tuned mass damper. Its maker says it can cut the tower's sway by up to forty percent.
During Typhoon Soudelor in twenty fifteen, the ball swung about one meter, the biggest move it has ever made.
And the best part? It is not hidden away. Visitors can walk right up to it and watch it work.
It even has its own cartoon mascots, called the Damper Babies. Yes, really.

chapters.title: Citicorp Center and the secret midnight repairs
chapters.short_title: The Skyscraper That Was Secretly Fixed at Night

beats.say: In nineteen seventy eight, one of New York's newest skyscrapers had a problem that almost nobody was allowed to know about.
Citicorp Center was fifty nine stories tall, and it stood on four giant stilts so a church could keep its corner of the block.
It was very light for its size, so the engineer, William LeMessurier, added a four hundred ton concrete block that floats on oil to calm the sway.
Then a student named Diane Hartley started asking questions about winds hitting the building from the corners.
LeMessurier checked again and found something worse. Joints that were meant to be welded had been bolted together instead.
His numbers said that if the power went out and the damper stopped, a strong enough storm could arrive about once every sixteen years.
So every night, after the office workers went home, welders slipped in and covered about two hundred joints with thick steel plates.
Then Hurricane Ella started heading up the coast, and the city quietly prepared evacuation plans just in case.
Luckily, the storm turned out to sea. The repairs were finished, and the story stayed mostly secret for almost twenty years.
And that student's question? It may have helped save a skyscraper.

chapters.title: Tokyo Skytree copies an ancient pagoda

beats.say: Tokyo Skytree is six hundred thirty four meters tall, in one of the most earthquake prone cities on Earth.
Its secret weapon is not new at all. It comes from wooden pagodas that are well over a thousand years old.
Old Japanese pagodas have a central pillar called a shinbashira, running up the middle of the building.
Skytree has its own version: a concrete column eight meters wide and three hundred seventy five meters tall, standing inside the steel tower.
Here is the clever bit. The column and the outer tower are built separately, so they shake at different rhythms.
When one leans left and the other leans right, they cancel each other out, a bit like two people steadying a canoe.
Oil dampers between them soak up the energy, like the shock absorbers in a car.
According to its designers, the system cuts earthquake shaking by up to half, and wind shaking by about thirty percent.
In twenty eleven, while still under construction, Skytree rode out the Great East Japan Earthquake without damage.
A thirteen hundred year old idea, holding up one of the tallest towers in the world.

chapters.title: Burj Khalifa confuses the wind
chapters.short_title: How the Burj Khalifa Confuses the Wind

beats.say: The Burj Khalifa is eight hundred twenty eight meters tall, and up there the wind is a serious bully.
The danger is not only the push. When wind flows around a tall tower, it peels off in swirls on alternating sides.
Those swirls are called vortices, and they tug the building left, then right, then left again.
If that rhythm matches the building's natural sway, the motion can build up, like pushing a kid on a swing at just the right moment.
So the designers did something sneaky. They made sure the tower never has the same shape for very long.
The building has three wings, and as it rises it steps inward in a spiral of setbacks, more than two dozen of them.
Every time the width changes, the swirls change too, so they never line up into one strong rhythm.
Its chief structural engineer, Bill Baker, calls this confusing the wind.
They even tested models in wind tunnels and rotated the whole building to face the strongest desert winds in its best direction.
The tallest building on Earth does not fight the wind. It just keeps it guessing.

chapters.title: Shanghai Tower twists to save millions
chapters.short_title: Why the Shanghai Tower Is Twisted

beats.say: The Shanghai Tower looks like someone grabbed the top and gave it a twist. That is exactly the point.
At six hundred thirty two meters, it is China's tallest building, in a city that gets typhoon force winds.
The glass skin rotates about one hundred twenty degrees from bottom to top, and it gets narrower as it rises.
Engineers tested different versions in a wind tunnel to see how much twist worked best.
The twist, the taper, and the rounded corners break up the wind before it can grab the building.
The result was about twenty four percent less wind load than a plain box tower of the same height.
Less wind load means less steel and concrete, which reportedly saved about fifty eight million dollars.
And just in case, there is also a giant damper near the top, a cousin of the ball inside Taipei 101.
So the twist is not only for looks. It is a shape that pays for itself.
Sometimes the smartest way to beat the wind is to stop standing in its way.

outro.say: A swinging ball, a secret repair, an ancient pillar, a confusing shape, and a twist that saves millions.
Skyscrapers do not win by being stiff. They win by being clever.
Which trick surprised you most? Tell us in the comments, and follow Simply Weird for more weird things, explained the fun way.
